stem: In a myelinated axon, where do action potentials occur?

options.content: Only at the nodes of Ranvier
options.rationale: Correct: the myelin insulates the rest of the axon.

options.content: Only under the Schwann cells
options.rationale: Myelin prevents ion flow there.

options.content: Along the whole length of the membrane
options.rationale: That is continuous conduction in unmyelinated axons.

options.content: Only at the synaptic knobs
options.rationale: Action potentials travel along the axon, not only at its end.

explanation: Depolarisation happens only at the **nodes of Ranvier**: saltatory conduction.

stem: Why does an impulse normally travel in only one direction along an axon?

options.content: The membrane behind the action potential is refractory
options.rationale: Correct: its sodium channels are inactivated.

options.content: Sodium ions can diffuse only towards the axon terminal
options.rationale: Ions diffuse both ways in local circuits.

options.content: The myelin sheath blocks backward movement of ions
options.rationale: Unmyelinated axons also conduct one way.

options.content: Voltage-gated channels are present only ahead of the impulse
options.rationale: Channels are present along the whole membrane.

explanation: The region behind is in its **refractory period**, so local currents can only depolarise the resting membrane ahead.

stem: Which change would increase the conduction velocity of an unmyelinated axon?

options.content: A decrease in temperature from 30 °C to 20 °C
options.rationale: Lower temperature slows ion diffusion.

options.content: A shorter length of axon
options.rationale: Length changes the time taken, not the speed.

options.content: An increase in axon diameter
options.rationale: Correct: less resistance to local currents.

options.content: A lower concentration of sodium ions outside
options.rationale: This would weaken depolarisation, not speed it up.

explanation: A wider axon offers less resistance to the flow of ions, so local currents spread further and faster.

stem: What makes the myelin sheath an effective electrical insulator?

options.content: It is made of a thick layer of cellulose
options.rationale: Myelin is membrane, not cellulose.

options.content: It contains many voltage-gated sodium ion channels along it
options.rationale: Channels are concentrated at the nodes, not in myelin.

options.content: It is a single layer of protein fibres
options.rationale: Myelin is many layers of Schwann cell membrane.

options.content: It consists of many layers of lipid-rich membrane
options.rationale: Correct: ions cannot cross the lipid layers.

explanation: Schwann cells wrap many layers of their phospholipid-rich membrane around the axon, preventing ion flow.

stem: In multiple sclerosis, patches of myelin are lost from some axons in the central nervous system. What is the most likely effect on impulses in those axons?

options.content: They travel faster because more membrane is exposed
options.rationale: Losing myelin removes saltatory conduction, slowing impulses.

options.content: They are slowed or fail to reach the next node
options.rationale: Correct: saltatory conduction is disrupted.

options.content: They become larger in amplitude along the axon
options.rationale: Action potentials are all-or-nothing.

options.content: They travel in both directions along the axon
options.rationale: The refractory period still prevents backward travel.

explanation: Without myelin, local currents leak and may not depolarise the next node to threshold, so impulses slow or stop.

stem: Which statement correctly describes a local circuit in an unmyelinated axon?

options.content: K⁺ is pumped along the inside of the axon to the next node
options.rationale: Local circuits involve diffusion, not pumping, and there are no nodes.

options.content: Na⁺ that entered diffuses inside the axon to the next resting region
options.rationale: Correct: this depolarises the neighbouring membrane.

options.content: Na⁺ moves along the outside of the myelin to the next node
options.rationale: There is no myelin on an unmyelinated axon.

options.content: Neurotransmitter diffuses along the inside of the axon to the next region
options.rationale: Neurotransmitter acts at synapses, not along axons.

explanation: Na⁺ diffuses sideways inside the axon, towards the negative resting region, depolarising it to threshold.

stem: Axon X is myelinated and 12 µm in diameter; axon Y is unmyelinated and 600 µm in diameter. Both are at 25 °C. Which prediction is most likely?

options.content: Y conducts faster than X because it is fifty times wider
options.rationale: Width helps, but saltatory conduction gives a far larger increase.

options.content: X and Y conduct at the same speed because the temperature is equal
options.rationale: Temperature is only one factor.

options.content: Y cannot conduct impulses because it has no myelin
options.rationale: Unmyelinated axons conduct, only more slowly.

options.content: X conducts faster than Y, despite its much smaller diameter
options.rationale: Correct: myelination has a larger effect than diameter.

explanation: A thin myelinated axon (tens of m s⁻¹) outpaces even a giant unmyelinated axon (about 20-25 m s⁻¹).
hints: Which factor has the bigger effect on speed?

stem: Saltatory conduction uses less ATP than continuous conduction over the same length of axon.
explanation: True. Ions cross the membrane only at the nodes, so the sodium-potassium pump has fewer ions to move back.

stem: A stronger stimulus is signalled by larger action potentials travelling along the axon.
explanation: False. Action potentials are all-or-nothing; a stronger stimulus gives a higher frequency (and often more neurones firing).

stem: Match each feature with its effect on transmission.
explanation: Myelin → saltatory; diameter → resistance; refractory → one-way; temperature → diffusion rate.

payload.template: In a myelinated axon, local circuits flow from one {{blank:a}} to the next, so the impulse jumps; this is called {{blank:b}} conduction.

stem: Name the type of conduction in which the impulse jumps from node to node.
Two electrodes are placed 84 mm apart on an axon. An impulse reaches the second electrode 1.4 ms after the first. Calculate the conduction velocity in m s⁻¹.
explanation:
1. Distance $= 84\ \text{mm} = 0.084\ \text{m}$; time $= 1.4\ \text{ms} = 0.0014\ \text{s}$.
2. Speed $= \dfrac{0.084}{0.0014} = 60\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
Converting only the distance (m ÷ ms) gives 0.06, which is wrong.
workedSolution:
1. Distance $= 84\ \text{mm} = 0.084\ \text{m}$; time $= 1.4\ \text{ms} = 0.0014\ \text{s}$.
2. Speed $= \dfrac{0.084}{0.0014} = 60\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
Converting only the distance (m ÷ ms) gives 0.06, which is wrong.
hints: Convert both distance and time to SI units.
1 mm per ms = 1 m per s.

stem: A motor neurone running from the spinal cord to a toe muscle is 1.05 m long and conducts at 70 m s⁻¹. Calculate the time, in ms, for an impulse to travel its full length.
explanation: Time $= \dfrac{1.05}{70} = 0.015\ \text{s} = 15\ \text{ms}$. Giving 0.015 forgets to convert to ms; dividing speed by length is the wrong way round.
workedSolution: 1. Time $= \dfrac{1.05}{70} = 0.015\ \text{s} = 15\ \text{ms}$. Giving 0.015 forgets to convert to ms; dividing speed by length is the wrong way round.

stem: Explain how an action potential is propagated along an unmyelinated axon.

points.description: Na⁺ that has entered at the action potential diffuses sideways inside the axon (local circuit)
This depolarises the neighbouring resting region of membrane
When threshold is reached, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open there and a new action potential is produced
The region behind is refractory, so the action potential moves forward only

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: At the site of an action potential, sodium ions that have entered diffuse sideways inside the axon towards the neighbouring resting region, forming a local circuit with the opposite movement of positive ions outside. This depolarises the neighbouring membrane, and when it reaches the threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open there and a new action potential is generated. The region behind is in its refractory period, so the wave of action potentials moves forward along the axon.

explanation: Local circuits, threshold, new action potential, refractory region behind.

stem: Suggest why vertebrates have many thin myelinated axons in their nerves, whereas squid rely on a few giant unmyelinated axons for rapid escape responses.

points.description: Myelinated axons conduct fast while staying thin
So many axons can be packed into a nerve / many different signals carried in a small space
Giant axons achieve speed through large diameter but take up much space, so only a few can be used (for essential escape reflexes) / myelination also saves ATP

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Myelination gives very fast saltatory conduction even in thin axons, so a vertebrate nerve can contain thousands of fast axons carrying different signals in a small space. Squid achieve speed by increasing diameter, which works but needs a lot of space, so only a few giant axons can be used, for vital escape responses. Myelinated axons also use less ATP per impulse.

explanation: Speed per unit space is the key comparison.
hints: Think about how much space each strategy needs.

stem: Describe three ways in which the refractory period is important in the transmission of impulses.

points.description: Ensures one-way transmission (region behind cannot be depolarised)
Ensures action potentials are discrete / separate and do not merge
Limits the maximum frequency of impulses

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The refractory period means the region behind an action potential cannot be re-excited, so impulses travel only one way. It keeps action potentials separate from each other so they do not merge. It also sets a maximum frequency at which impulses can be sent.

stem:
Rudo measured the time for an impulse to travel 50 mm along an isolated frog nerve at different temperatures.

| Temperature / °C | Time / ms |
|---|---|
| 10 | 2.5 |
| 15 | 2 |
| 20 | 1.5 |
| 25 | 1.25 |
| 30 | 1 |
| 35 | 0.75 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the conduction velocity at 20 °C in m s⁻¹. Give your answer to three significant figures.
parts.explanation: $\dfrac{50\ \text{mm}}{1.5\ \text{ms}} = 33.33\ \text{mm ms}^{-1} = 33.3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (3 s.f.). Dividing by 1000 as well gives 0.0333, which is wrong because 1 mm ms⁻¹ already equals 1 m s⁻¹.
parts.workedSolution: 1. $\dfrac{50\ \text{mm}}{1.5\ \text{ms}} = 33.33\ \text{mm ms}^{-1} = 33.3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (3 s.f.). Dividing by 1000 as well gives 0.0333, which is wrong because 1 mm ms⁻¹ already equals 1 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage increase in conduction velocity from 10 °C to 35 °C. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.explanation: Speeds: $50 \div 2.5 = 20$ and $50 \div 0.75 = 66.67\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Increase $= \dfrac{66.67 - 20}{20} \times 100 = 233.3 \approx 233\%$. Dividing by 66.67 instead gives 70%, which is wrong.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Speeds: $50 \div 2.5 = 20$ and $50 \div 0.75 = 66.67\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Increase $= \dfrac{66.67 - 20}{20} \times 100 = 233.3 \approx 233\%$. Dividing by 66.67 instead gives 70%, which is wrong.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain the effect of temperature shown by these results.

points.description: Speed increases with temperature (time falls from 2.5 ms to 0.75 ms)
Ions diffuse faster / channels open and close faster at higher temperature (more kinetic energy), so local circuits depolarise the next region sooner

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: As temperature rose from 10 °C to 35 °C, the time fell from 2.5 ms to 0.75 ms, so speed increased. Ions have more kinetic energy and diffuse faster, so local currents depolarise the next region to threshold sooner.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Predict what would happen to the conduction velocity if the nerve were heated to 55 °C, and explain.

points.description: Speed falls / conduction stops, because channel proteins and pumps denature

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Conduction would slow or stop, because channel and pump proteins denature at high temperature.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: State one variable Rudo should have kept constant.

points.description: Same nerve / same distance between electrodes / same stimulus strength / same saline (ion concentration)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The distance between the electrodes (or the same nerve, stimulus strength or saline solution).

explanation: Speed = distance ÷ time; temperature speeds diffusion until proteins denature.
hints: 50 mm ÷ time in ms gives m s⁻¹ directly.

stem:
The table shows the conduction velocity of four axons.

| Axon | Diameter / µm | Myelinated? | Velocity / m s⁻¹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 2 | No | 1.5 |
| B | 2 | Yes | 12 |
| C | 15 | Yes | 90 |
| D | 400 | No | 18 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: How many times faster does axon B conduct than axon A?

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Use axons A and B to explain the effect of myelination on conduction velocity.

points.description: Same diameter, so the difference is due to myelin (B is 8 times faster)
Myelin insulates, so depolarisation occurs only at nodes of Ranvier
Local circuits span from node to node / saltatory conduction, which is faster than depolarising every part of the membrane

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A and B have the same diameter, so the eightfold difference in speed is due to myelination. In B the myelin insulates the axon, so action potentials occur only at the nodes of Ranvier; local circuits extend from node to node and the impulse jumps between them (saltatory conduction), which is much faster than depolarising each patch of membrane in turn as in A.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Compare axons C and D and explain what the comparison shows.

points.description: C is much thinner (15 vs 400 µm) yet faster (90 vs 18 m s⁻¹)
Shows myelination has a greater effect than diameter / D relies on large diameter (lower resistance) alone

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: C is about 27 times thinner than D but conducts five times faster (90 compared with 18 m s⁻¹). This shows that myelination increases speed far more than diameter does; D depends only on its large diameter, which lowers resistance to local currents.

explanation: Control one factor to compare the other.
hints: Which pair differs in only one factor?
